doctrines.name: Manipular Drill
doctrines.historical_note: Rome abandoned the hoplite phalanx during the Samnite Wars (343-290 BC), whose hill country punished a rigid line. The three-line manipular array of hastati, principes and triarii could open, close and relieve itself in mid-battle.
doctrines.description: Maniples that open and close on command. Infantry stand a little firmer and keep their order on broken ground.

doctrines.name: Iberian Sword Pattern
doctrines.historical_note: The gladius hispaniensis, a cut-and-thrust sword copied from Iberian mercenaries and enemies during the Second Punic War, became the legion's standard blade for two centuries.
doctrines.description: Adopt the enemy's better sword: infantry strike harder. Learned only from fighting foot soldiers.

doctrines.name: Pilum Volley
doctrines.historical_note: A volley of heavy javelins thrown at twenty paces, bending in the shield it pierced, broke the momentum of a charge before the swords came out; at Telamon (225 BC) and Zama (202 BC) it was the legion's opening argument.
doctrines.description: Every legionary carries the pilum: a charge, mounted or on foot, is disordered before it lands.

doctrines.name: Engineering Corps
doctrines.historical_note: Roman armies dug as much as they fought: the double ring of works around Alesia (52 BC), the circumvallation of Numantia (133 BC), the ramp at Masada. Siege equipment came out of the legion's own ranks.
doctrines.description: Siege works go up a turn faster and assaults on prepared walls carry further.

doctrines.name: Camp Discipline
doctrines.historical_note: Polybius (Book VI) marvelled that a Roman army built the same fortified camp every night of a march. A beaten army had somewhere to rally, a tired one still fought, and citizens under such discipline resented the levy less.
doctrines.description: The nightly camp: forced marches no longer exhaust the men, beaten units rally rather than scatter, and the levy sits lighter on your towns.

doctrines.name: Cohort Reform
doctrines.historical_note: The reforms attributed to Gaius Marius (107 BC): the property qualification dropped, the cohort replacing the maniple, state-issued equipment, and long-service professionals who carried their own kit and called themselves his mules.
doctrines.description: Professional cohorts: infantry hit and hold harder and take the field already drilled. Requires the professional-army era.

doctrines.name: Mail Armour
doctrines.historical_note: The riveted mail shirt was a Celtic invention of the third century BC; Rome copied it as the lorica hamata and wore it for the next four hundred years. It needs iron, and a great deal of a smith's time.
doctrines.description: Mail shirts for the line: infantry and spearmen take fewer wounds. Needs a region that yields iron.

doctrines.name: Sarissa Drill
doctrines.historical_note: Philip II gave Macedon the sarissa, a two-handed pike of five to six metres, and drilled poor farmers until sixteen ranks could move as one. His son took it to the Indus.
doctrines.description: The Macedonian phalanx drilled to move as one: pike blocks hold firmer and horses die on the points.

doctrines.name: Hoplite Tradition
doctrines.historical_note: The citizen hoplite with his round aspis and thrusting spear won Marathon (490 BC) and Plataea (479 BC) and defined Greek war for three centuries: a wall of shields that horsemen would not charge.
doctrines.description: Citizen spearmen who have drilled in the shield wall since boyhood: firmer against horse and in the push of spears.

doctrines.name: Companion Wedge
doctrines.historical_note: Philip's and Alexander's Companion cavalry charged in a wedge, the point aimed at a seam in the enemy line: Chaeronea (338 BC) and Gaugamela (331 BC) were decided by it, with the phalanx as the anvil.
doctrines.description: Heavy horse trained to charge in a wedge: harder charges that find the seams in an infantry line.

doctrines.name: Torsion Artillery
doctrines.historical_note: Torsion catapults, powered by twisted sinew, appear under Dionysius I of Syracuse (c. 399 BC); by the siege of Rhodes (305 BC) Hellenistic engineers were building them by the hundred, and every city wall answered with its own.
doctrines.description: Bolt and stone throwers of the latest pattern: artillery hits harder, assaults carry further, and your own walls shoot back.

doctrines.name: Thureophoroi Reform
doctrines.historical_note: After Cynoscephalae (197 BC) and Pydna (168 BC) showed what broken ground did to a pike block, Greek states raised looser-order thureophoroi with the oval shield and trained the phalanx to keep its intervals on a slope. Learned from a defeat.
doctrines.description: Looser order for rough country: infantry and pikes keep their footing on hills and in woods. Available after a defeat.

doctrines.name: Elephant Corps
doctrines.historical_note: The Seleucids kept a permanent elephant corps from Indian stock; four hundred beasts screened the flanks at Ipsus (301 BC), and Raphia (217 BC) saw the only recorded battle between African and Indian elephants.
doctrines.description: A standing elephant establishment with mahouts and stables: steadier beasts, deadlier against foot, cheaper to keep.

doctrines.name: Falx Reapers
doctrines.historical_note: The Thracian rhomphaia and the Dacian falx, long curved blades swung two-handed, cut through shields and helmets; Trajan's legions added iron reinforcing bars to their helmets because of them.
doctrines.description: Two-handed blades that reach over a shield rim: infantry cut through spear and sword lines alike.

doctrines.name: Composite Bow Mastery
doctrines.historical_note: The recurved composite bow of horn, wood and sinew, drawn from the saddle, was the weapon of the Iranian plateau and the steppe. At Carrhae (53 BC) Surena's archers emptied their quivers into seven legions and were resupplied by camel.
doctrines.description: Horse archers who have shot from the saddle since childhood loose heavier, faster volleys.

doctrines.name: Cataphract Armour
doctrines.historical_note: Rider and horse both sheathed in scale, the Parthian and Armenian cataphract charged with a lance held in both hands. It took iron by the ton and broke Roman infantry at Carrhae; at Magnesia (190 BC) the Seleucid version routed a legion before being cut off.
doctrines.description: Man and horse in scale: heavy cavalry that shrugs off blows and rides through infantry. Needs iron.

doctrines.name: Parthian Shot
doctrines.historical_note: The feigned flight, turning in the saddle to shoot at the pursuer, meant a Parthian army was almost never caught: Crassus lost his at Carrhae (53 BC), Antony lost a third of his in retreat (36 BC), and neither ever brought the enemy to a decisive battle.
doctrines.description: Retreat is a manoeuvre: your beaten armies get away, and horse archers punish anyone who follows.

doctrines.name: Remount Herds
doctrines.historical_note: The Nisaean plain of Media bred the great horses of the East; a Parthian noble rode to war with a string of remounts, and an army so mounted moved and fought at a pace no infantry could match.
doctrines.description: State horse herds: mounted units cost less to keep and every army marches a little further. Needs horse country.

doctrines.name: Mercenary Contracts
doctrines.historical_note: Carthage fought with hired Libyans, Iberians, Gauls, Balearic slingers and Numidian horse under a small Punic officer corps. The Spartan Xanthippus, hired in 255 BC, beat Regulus outside the city with them.
doctrines.description: A standing network of recruiting agents: mercenaries sign on for less.

doctrines.name: Numidian Horsemanship
doctrines.historical_note: Numidian light horse rode without saddle or bridle, harried a marching enemy for days and turned every victory into a massacre: Hannibal's at Cannae (216 BC), and when Masinissa changed sides, Scipio's at Zama (202 BC).
doctrines.description: Light horse that never stop: your victories become routs and your defeats become escapes. Needs horse country.

doctrines.name: War Elephants
doctrines.historical_note: The forest elephants of the Atlas were Carthage's answer to the Hellenistic corps: thirty-seven crossed the Alps with Hannibal in 218 BC, and they scattered the Roman horse at the Trebia that winter.
doctrines.description: Stables and mahouts for the Atlas elephants: steadier beasts, deadlier against foot, cheaper to keep.

doctrines.name: Sacred Band Drill
doctrines.historical_note: The Sacred Band was Carthage's one native regiment: sons of the great houses, armoured and drilled as hoplites, who died almost to a man at the Crimissus (341 BC) rather than break.
doctrines.description: Citizen spearmen drilled as a sacred regiment: spear units hold and endure like the Band.

doctrines.name: Ptolemaic Phalanx
doctrines.historical_note: The Ptolemies settled Macedonian and Greek soldiers on Nile land in return for service, and drilled them in the sarissa; at Raphia (217 BC) that phalanx, stiffened with twenty thousand Egyptians, broke the Seleucid centre.
doctrines.description: Settler-soldiers drilled in the Macedonian manner: pikes and spears hold harder and turn back horse.

doctrines.name: Machimoi Levy
doctrines.historical_note: Ptolemy IV armed twenty thousand native Egyptians for Raphia and won; within a decade the machimoi who had learned to fight were in revolt, and Upper Egypt was lost to the crown for twenty years.
doctrines.description: Arm the native levy: cheap spears and infantry, but towns that have been drilled to fight remember it. The levy strains order far more.

doctrines.name: Nile Logistics
doctrines.historical_note: Grain, men and news moved on the river faster than on any road; an Egyptian army marched supplied and its garrisons were never far from relief.
doctrines.description: River supply: armies march a little further and garrisons keep order better, knowing the barges are behind them.

doctrines.name: Warband Fury
doctrines.historical_note: The Gallic charge, screaming and half naked, broke the Roman army at the Allia (390 BC) and nearly did so again at Telamon (225 BC): everything staked on the first rush.
doctrines.description: The first rush is everything: your armies hit harder when they attack.

doctrines.name: Woodland Ambush
doctrines.historical_note: The Boii annihilated two legions in the Litana forest (216 BC) by felling half-cut trees onto the column; Arminius did the same to three in the Teutoburg (AD 9). Both had served with Rome first and knew how it marched.
doctrines.description: Fight where the trees are: foot soldiers of every kind are deadlier in forest. Learned from facing infantry.

doctrines.name: Hill-Fort Engineering
doctrines.historical_note: The murus gallicus, timber-laced stone that neither ram nor fire could break, ringed the oppida of Gaul; Caesar at Alesia (52 BC) chose to starve Vercingetorix rather than storm it.
doctrines.description: Timber-laced walls: your garrisons fight better from them. Needs walls of the second tier.

doctrines.name: Chariot Tradition
doctrines.historical_note: Caesar found the war chariot still alive in Britain in 55 BC: drivers who could run along the pole at the gallop, warriors who dismounted to fight and remounted to flee, and Roman skirmishers who could not catch them.
doctrines.description: Charioteers bred to it: harder charges that run down skirmishers.

doctrines.name: Horse Lords
doctrines.historical_note: The Scythians and their Sarmatian successors lived in the saddle; Darius could not catch them in 513 BC and neither could anyone else. Every family bred its own remounts.
doctrines.description: A people on horseback: horse archers cost less and rule the steppe. Needs horse country.

doctrines.name: Veteran Cadres
doctrines.historical_note: Rome's evocati, veterans recalled to stiffen new legions, and the Hellenistic argyraspides show the same idea: seed every new unit with men who have seen a battle.
doctrines.description: Veterans train the recruits: every new unit starts a chevron wiser. Available after five victories.

doctrines.name: Drill Yards
doctrines.historical_note: A regular dilectus with drill fields in every town turned the levy from an outrage into a habit; a drilled garrison policed the streets it had grown up in.
doctrines.description: Regular drill in every town: garrisons keep order better and the levy is resented less. Needs barracks of the third tier.

doctrines.name: Armourers' Guild
doctrines.historical_note: State arms works — the Hellenistic royal arsenals and, later, the Roman fabricae — standardised patterns and let a city issue better kit than any private smith could.
doctrines.description: Standard patterns across the realm: your towns can issue one further level of weapon and armour upgrades. Needs an armoury of the second tier and iron.

doctrines.name: Siege Train
doctrines.historical_note: Demetrius the Besieger brought a nine-storey siege tower to Rhodes in 305 BC; a kingdom that kept its engines and engineers together opened a siege in days rather than months.
doctrines.description: Engines and engineers kept together: siege works are ready a turn sooner.
